v1123: Combine them into a short mission statement
v1124: Pray together for five minutes each night
v1125: Bless each other with a short prayer before work
v1126: Review the mission every three months
v1127: The gospel gives marriages a purpose bigger than themselves. "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it" (Psalm 127:1). Jesus promised, "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Matthew 18:20). When Prakash and Jyoti pray together, they invite God into the centre of their relationship. "A threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Their mission statement, "To love God, welcome others and raise children who know they are loved," helps them make decisions about money and time. Praying together also brings them into the presence of a loving Father, where they can be honest and receive grace as a couple.
v1128: God designed us to find meaning in shared purpose. Research suggests that couples who pray together report greater closeness and trust, perhaps because prayer involves vulnerability and shared attention. When two people share a vision, the brain's motivation systems align, and small sacrifices feel worthwhile. Regular blessing and prayer also signal safety and acceptance, which calm the nervous system. A clear mission reduces conflict by giving a shared reference point for decisions. God made marriage to reflect his own partnership with his people, which is always purposeful.
v1129: Ecclesiastes 4:12|A threefold cord is not quickly broken.
v1133: It took them three evenings to agree on their mission statement, and they argued about wording. Their nightly prayer is sometimes skipped when they are exhausted. But they now pray together most nights and bless each other each morning. They have found a balance between saving and giving, and they feel more like a team.
v1134: A shared purpose and shared prayer can turn two people into one team.
v1135: Prakash and Jyoti wrote down what their family is about and started praying together. Now they feel like they are on the same team.
v1136: The Body Log That Found the Hidden Stress
v1137: Neha, 32, a marketing executive in Delhi
v1138: Neha's body was always tense. Her shoulders ached, her jaw clenched and she woke at three most nights. She told herself she was fine. Her life looked calm, with a good job, a kind husband and no big problems. Her doctor checked her thyroid and blood count, which were normal, and suggested she track her symptoms. Neha started a seven-day body log, noting tension, sleep, food and events. By day four, she noticed a pattern. Her jaw clenched every evening between nine and ten, the time her manager sent messages on the office WhatsApp group. She also skipped lunch most days and drank four cups of tea. She had never connected the two.
v1139: Research suggests the body can stay in stress mode when there is a hidden, ongoing stressor. Neha did not consciously think of the evening messages as stressful, but her nervous system did. Each ping signalled possible criticism, and her stress response switched on. Her body never had time to recover because the trigger came every night. Skipping meals and drinking lots of caffeine added to the strain, with blood sugar dips and extra adrenaline. Neha's father had been demanding, and she learned to stay alert for his moods. Her body had carried that alertness into her adult work life.
v1140: During a quiet time Neha read Psalm 139:23, "Search me, O God, and know my heart." She realised God cared about her body and her hidden stress, and she asked him to show her what she could change.
v1141: Keep a seven-day body log of tension, sleep, food and events
v1142: Mute the office group after eight in the evening
v1143: Eat lunch and cut down to two cups of tea
v1144: Do a short body scan and prayer before bed
v1145: Talk with her manager about evening messages
v1146: God knows our bodies and cares about our stress. "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psalm 139:23). Neha found that inviting God to search her life led her to discover what was hidden. Jesus told his tired disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Her body was "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 6:19), worthy of care. God is a faithful Father who does not demand endless availability. Talking honestly with her manager and husband also helped, because she no longer carried the stress alone. Grace freed her from the belief that she must always respond instantly to be acceptable.
v1147: God designed the stress response to help us face real danger, then return to rest. Research suggests that small, repeated stressors can keep the HPA axis switched on, especially when we do not notice them. A body log helps the thinking brain see patterns the body has been reacting to. Once Neha identified the trigger, she could set a boundary and let her body complete the stress cycle. God also designed us to need regular meals, sleep and recovery. Caring for these basics helps the nervous system feel safe.
v1148: Psalm 139:23|Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts.
v1152: Within a month Neha's jaw clenching reduced, and she slept through most nights. Her manager agreed to send non-urgent messages in the morning. She still feels tense during busy weeks and sometimes forgets lunch. But she knows what to look for now, and she keeps a short log whenever her body starts to feel tight again.
v1153: A hidden stressor can keep the body on alert until we look for it with honesty and care.
v1154: Neha's body felt tight all the time. She wrote down how she felt each day and found that late work messages were stressing her, so she turned them off.
v1155: The Racing Heart That Was Not Only Stress
v1157: Ajay's heart raced constantly. He felt jittery, sweated easily and lost five kilos without trying. His hands trembled when he held his tea cup. It was audit season, and he assumed it was work stress. His friend at church said he should pray more and worry less. Ajay prayed, but the symptoms got worse. He could not sleep and snapped at his wife and children. One day, climbing stairs, he felt so breathless and shaky he had to sit down. His wife insisted he see a doctor. Blood tests showed an overactive thyroid. The doctor explained that his thyroid was pushing his body into overdrive, and work stress was adding fuel to the fire.
v1158: Research suggests that physical conditions such as an overactive thyroid, anaemia, blood sugar problems or sleep apnoea can cause symptoms that feel just like anxiety and stress. An overactive thyroid speeds up the heart, raises body temperature and makes the nervous system feel on edge. In Ajay's case, real work stress and a physical illness were both present. He had grown up believing that a strong man ignores his body, because his father worked through illness and never complained. So Ajay pushed on, and his body kept getting louder. Shame about needing help made him delay.
v1159: While waiting for his test results, Ajay read 3 John 1:2, about prospering and being in health. He realised God cared about his body as well as his soul, and that seeing a doctor was not a lack of faith.
v1160: See a doctor and get blood tests to rule out physical causes
v1161: Take treatment as prescribed for the thyroid
v1162: Lower caffeine and add gentle walks
v1163: Share the workload during audit season with his team
v1164: Rest one evening a week without work
v1165: The gospel speaks to the whole person, body and soul. "I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (3 John 1:2). Seeking medical care is part of stewarding the body God gave us. Luke was "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14), and Jesus healed many physical illnesses. Ajay learned that faith and medicine work together. He also learned that he did not have to prove his strength by suffering silently. God is a Father who cares for our needs, and Christ understands our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). Accepting help from his doctor, his wife and his team was a step of humility and trust.
v1166: God designed the body with many systems that talk to each other. The thyroid gland controls how fast the body uses energy. When it is overactive, it speeds up the heart and nervous system, much like the stress response does. Research suggests that physical causes can make anxiety symptoms worse and can make it hard for the body to calm down. Treating the underlying cause, along with managing stress, allows the body to return to balance. God made us to need both care for our bodies and rest for our souls.
v1167: 3 John 1:2|I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
v1171: After two months of thyroid treatment, Ajay's heart rate settled and his weight stabilised. Work stress still makes him tense, but the overwhelming jitteriness is gone. He had a setback when he stopped his medicine too early and his symptoms returned. Now he keeps regular check-ups and has learned to listen to his body sooner.
v1172: Sometimes stress has a physical cause, and caring for our bodies is part of faithful living.
v1173: Ajay's heart beat too fast, and he thought it was just stress. A doctor found a thyroid problem, and medicine and rest helped him feel better.
v1174: The Pastor Who Could Not Relax
v1175: Pastor Imli, 52, who leads a church in Dimapur, Nagaland
v1176: Pastor Imli finally took his first holiday in four years, a week with his wife in Shillong. But he could not relax. He checked his phone every hour, worried about the church, and woke at dawn with his mind racing about sermons and members' problems. By day three he had a headache and felt guilty for resting while others were working. On Sunday he felt restless all morning, wondering who was preaching and how it was going. His wife said, "You are here, but not really here." He realised that even on Sundays at home he never truly rested. Ministry was always on his mind. He felt tired all the time, yet he could not stop.
v1177: Research suggests that when the body lives in stress mode for years, it can forget how to switch off. The stress response stays on, even during holidays or quiet moments. Pastors often carry many people's burdens and rarely have time to recover. Pastor Imli also grew up as the son of a village elder who said a good leader never rests. He learned that his worth came from being needed. When he tried to rest, his nervous system felt it as danger, as if something terrible would happen if he stopped watching. Carrying everything alone and feeling guilty about rest kept his body stuck.
v1178: On the holiday, Pastor Imli read about Elijah under the juniper tree, where an angel said, "Arise and eat." He realised God cared for Elijah's tired body before giving him more work. God was inviting him to rest too.
v1179: Turn off his phone for set hours on holiday
v1180: Hand over church duties fully to trusted elders
v1181: Take a weekly Sabbath with no ministry tasks
v1182: Do a gentle evening downshift routine
v1183: Pray and simply be with God without preparing sermons
v1184: The gospel tells pastors that they are sheep before they are shepherds. Jesus is the Good Shepherd, and the church belongs to him. "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters" (Psalm 23:2). God cared for Elijah's exhaustion with food, sleep and gentle presence (1 Kings 19:5). Jesus invited his disciples to "rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Sabbath is God's gift, not a reward for finishing work. Pastor Imli did not have to earn God's love by being always available. Sharing leadership with elders also reflected the body of Christ, where every member has a part. Rest became an act of faith that God is holding everything.
v1185: God designed us with rhythms of work and rest. Research suggests that without regular recovery, the stress system stays switched on, leading to exhaustion and burnout. The body needs time to complete the stress cycle through movement, rest, sleep and connection. Sabbath gives the nervous system a weekly chance to reset. When pastors rest, their brains can recover, their creativity returns and they serve with more joy. God built rest into creation from the beginning, and he himself rested on the seventh day.
v1186: Psalm 23:2|He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
v1190: Pastor Imli's next holiday went better. He switched off his phone for most of each day and enjoyed walks with his wife. He now takes Mondays as his Sabbath. Some weeks, crises still pull him back, and he feels guilty when resting. But the elders are carrying more responsibility, and he says he feels closer to God than he has in years.
v1191: Rest is not laziness but trust that God holds what we cannot.
v1192: Pastor Imli could not stop worrying about church, even on holiday. He learned that God takes care of the church, so he can rest.
v1193: Wired but Tired With a New Baby
v1194: Rebecca, 29, a first-time mother of an eight-month-old in Thrissur, Kerala
v1195: Rebecca was exhausted all day but could not sleep at night. Even when her baby slept, her mind raced and her body buzzed. She drank coffee to get through mornings and scrolled her phone late into the night. She felt irritable and cried easily. She thought she should be grateful and happy, which made her feel guilty. Her husband, George, worked long hours and assumed she was fine because she never asked for help. One afternoon she nearly fell asleep while feeding the baby on the sofa. Frightened, she called her sister and admitted she was not coping. Her sister came to stay for a week and encouraged her to see a doctor.
